sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2.5 km around Uptown Charlotte (35.2271, -80.8431)

stops.name: Liddell-McNinch House
stops.description: President William Howard Taft was entertained in this Queen Anne house in 1909, back when Fourth Ward was a residential neighborhood rather than a pocket of survivors among the towers.

stops.name: Old Settlers' Cemetery
stops.description: Charlotte's first public burial ground holds graves from 1776 to 1884, including Thomas Polk, the town founder whose great-nephew James K. Polk became president.

stops.name: Carolina Theatre
stops.description: This 1927 movie palace hosted Elvis Presley and Bob Hope, went dark in 1978, then sat empty for nearly half a century before reopening in March 2025 after a restoration.

stops.name: Discovery Place Science
stops.description: Charlotte's science museum grew out of a schoolteacher's small collection founded in 1946 and now runs the largest IMAX Dome theater in the Carolinas.

stops.name: First Presbyterian Church
stops.description: The Gothic Revival sanctuary dates to 1857, but its spire was rebuilt in the 1880s and its side and rear walls replaced in the 1890s, so the church is a nineteenth-century building in three installments.

stops.name: Charles R. Jonas Federal Building
stops.description: Finished in 1915 as Charlotte's post office and federal courthouse, it was traded to the city in 2005 and immediately leased back to the government that built it.

stops.name: Johnston Building
stops.description: Charlotte's tallest building from 1924 to 1926, this office tower started at 15 stories, later gained two more, and only reached the National Register in 2025.

stops.name: Latta Arcade
stops.description: The skylight over this 1914 shopping arcade was not decorative: cotton buyers needed daylight to grade samples on the atrium floor.

stops.name: Home Federal Building
stops.description: A 1967 International Style bank tower that kept its original fountain, pool and walkway bridge, now converted to condominiums and one of uptown's few listed modernist buildings.

stops.name: Bechtler Museum of Modern Art
stops.description: Swiss architect Mario Botta designed this museum around one family's collection of more than 1,400 mid-century modern works, assembled and inherited by a Charlotte resident born in Switzerland.

stops.name: Mint Museum Uptown
stops.description: The uptown half of a museum that began in the old Charlotte branch of the U.S. Mint, five stories built for craft, design, American and contemporary art.

stops.name: St. Peter's Catholic Church
stops.description: Established in 1851, this is the oldest Catholic church in Charlotte and it now sits mid-block among the glass of the arts district.

stops.name: Harvey B. Gantt Center for African-American Arts + Culture
stops.description: Named for the first Black student at Clemson, who later became Charlotte's first Black mayor, this four-story center opened in 2009 as the newest piece of the Levine Center for the Arts.

stops.name: Romare Bearden Park
stops.description: The layout of this 5.4-acre park is drawn from the collages of Romare Bearden, a Charlotte-born artist, and it faces the Knights' ballpark across the street.

stops.name: NASCAR Hall of Fame
stops.address: 400 E Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
stops.description: Charlotte won the bid for this hall in 2006 and opened it in 2010; seventy drivers, owners, crew chiefs and broadcasters have been enshrined so far.

stops.name: Mecklenburg Investment Company Building
stops.description: This narrow 1922 brick office block was built in the Brooklyn neighborhood as a home for Charlotte's Black professionals and is tied to the New Negro movement.

stops.name: Grace A.M.E. Zion Church
stops.description: Built in 1901 by William W. Smith, a Black contractor, this Gothic Revival church with two mismatched entry towers is one of the few buildings left from the razed Brooklyn neighborhood.

note: Charlotte, NC - never run before; Atlanta, Baltimore, Boston and Buffalo have all had turns. All 17 stops sit inside the I-277 loop in Uptown and form roughly a 1.2-mile figure-eight: Fourth Ward, down the Tryon Street spine to the Levine Center for the Arts, then east to Brevard Street. Every stop was confirmed still standing and street-visible from its own article. Dropped as demolished, though still listed on the NRHP county page: Independence Building (100-102 W Trade), Hotel Charlotte (327 W Trade), Merchants and Farmers National Bank Building (123 E Trade). Also dropped: Thomas Polk Park, because the 1993 park at Trade and Tryon was approved in 2023 for a redesign and renaming after Hugh McColl, so what stands there now is not what the article describes; and Levine Museum of the New South, whose 401 S Tryon space closed in May 2025 and which is moving to 1800 South Blvd in South End, outside the walkable core. Skipped as out-of-cluster despite good articles: Bank of America Stadium, Truist Field, the Seaboard Air Line passenger station on N Tryon, and the W Morehead St mill buildings. Every stop has a street address and a ZIP; Uptown Charlotte is entirely 28202. Addresses come from the NRHP listing rows or the article infoboxes, never from coordinates. Mint Museum Uptown has no article of its own, so its source_url is the Mint Museum article covering both campuses.
